[MESSAGE FROM THE AUDITOR-GENERAL]

I t is my privilege and honour to present the Office of the Auditor-General's (OAG) Annual Corporate Report for 2024/2025. This report is in compliance with Article 254 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya, which requires that after the end of each financial year, a holder of an Independent Office submits a report to the President and to Parliament on the operations.

The report provides an overview of the achievements, activities, challenges and financial performance of OAG over the year. It also highlights initiatives aimed at enhancing collaboration and engagements between the Office and our stakeholders. This report is a testament of our joint efforts in enhancing accountability and safeguarding public funds for the benefit of all Kenyans.

[Our audits]

We submitted 2,746 financial audit reports to Parliament and County Assemblies, comprising 1,785 reports for National Government entities and 961 for County Governments' entities. We also issued twenty-seven (27) special audit reports on thematic areas of public interest. AUDIT REPORT

Additionally, we gave technical support to Committees of Parliament during discussions on the reports.

Our Performance Audit reports continue to receive attention and interest from Parliament and other stakeholders and we are delighted that the second performance audit report, on Response to Floods in Kenya, was discussed by the National Assembly's Departmental Committee on Regional Development.

The first ever Performance audit report to be discussed by Parliament was  on Provision of Services to Persons with Disability . We continue to engage Parliament to prioritise discussion of Performance Audit reports because they touch on various critical sectors and provide recommendations which, if implemented will mitigate against some of the current issues or challanges we are experiencing as a country.

[transparency of public financial reporting.]

While we recognize the achievements of the past year, we also acknowledge the challenges we faced. These included inadequate resources, adapting to emerging issues, expanding audit scope and the growing demand for quality and timely audits. Addressing these challenges requires

sustained support from all our stakeholders.

[Stakeholder engagement]

To effectively respond to stakeholders' expectations for impact, we initiated and sustained stakeholder engagement through continuous dialogue with the Executive, Parliament, County Governments, Media, Audited entities, Development Partners, Civil Society Organisations and citizens, among other stakeholders.

Citizens are strategic stakeholders in the oversight of prudent management and use of public resources. To this end, we conduct participatory audits, where citizens, through Civil Society Organisations are involved in the audit process to enhance accountability.

Additionally, we are reviewing the Citizen Accountability Audit Engagement Framework to respond to the emerging needs of the citizens on accountability

[Our commitment]

We commit to continue delivering

on our mandate guided by our core values of Integrity, Credibility, Relevance, Accountability and Independence.

Further, we leverage the use of technology

and data analytics to enhance efficiency in our audit services.

I thank my staff for their dedication and professionalism in ensuring that every shilling is accounted for. I also appreciate the contributions and support of our stakeholders in enhancing public sector accountability.

T he Office of the Auditor-General (OAG) is an Independent Office established by Article 229 of the Constitution of Kenya. The Office is charged with the primary oversight role of ensuring accountability in the use of public resources within the three arms of government (the Legislature, the Judiciary and the Executive) as well as the Constitutional Commissions, Independent Offices and any entity that is funded from public funds.

Our mandate is guided by the following pieces of Legislation:

[229(4 )]

Focuses on the audit of accounts of all entities funded from public funds, with respect to financial accountability.

[249 (1)]

Gives the Auditor-General, alongside other Independent Offices and Commissions, the power to:(a) protect the sovereignty of the people; (b) secure the observance by all State Organs of democratic values and principles; and

(c) promote constitutionalism.

The mandate of the Office is further expounded by the Public Audit Act, 2015.

[229(6)]

Focuses on the aspect of lawfulness and effectiveness in the use of public resources. We address compliance in the use of public resources.  We also address the impact on the use of public resources by conducting Performance Audits or Value for Money Audits by looking at the efficiency, economy and effectiveness on the use and management of public funds for the benefit of the people.

[252]

We conduct investigations on complaints made by members of the public and conduct conciliation, mediation and arbitrations on matters related to public financial management.

[Strategic Focus]

The Office's strategic direction is guided by the OAG Strategic Plan 2021-2026. The Plan emphasises on conducting impactful audits that contribute to improving the lives and livelihoods of citizens. It aligns with International Organisation of Supreme Audit Institutions (INTOSAI's) Framework for Professional Pronouncements Principle 12, which emphasises on Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) demonstrating their value and benefits to the public.

The strategic direction is anchored on three priorities:

[Our Audits]

During the year, we conducted the following audits:

[Financial Audits]

These audits examine and evaluate financial statements of public entities to confirm whether they present a true and fair view and transparent disclosure of transactions.

We carried out 2,746 financial audits comprising 1,785 at the National level and 961 at the County level, as indicated:

We continue to improve the effectiveness and quality of the audit process to ensure that the audit reports and recommendations are credible, relevant, reliable and value adding. This is geared towards influencing improved decision-making and positive impact on the lives and livelihoods of citizens.

[Audit Opinions]

The Auditor-General expresses opinions on the financial statements depending on the level of transparency, accountability and disclosure as follows;

[1. Unmodified/Unqualified Opinion]

This means that the books of accounts and the supporting records agree with the financial statements presented and no material misstatements have been found. The financial statements present fairly, in all material respects the operations of the audited entity.

[2. Qualified Opinion]

This means that the recorded financial transactions are to a large extent in agreement with the underlying records, except for cases where material misstatements or omissions in the financial statements are noted. The issues, though deemed material, are not widespread or persistent.

[3.  Adverse Opinion]

This opinion is issued where financial statements exhibit significant misstatements from the underlying accounting records. The financial statements significantly disagree with the underlying books of accounts and/or standards. The problems are widespread, persistent and require considerable interventions by management for rectification.

[4. Disclaimer of Opinion]

3

The Auditor-General witholds an opinion issued when financial statements exhibit serious and significant misstatements that may arise from inadequate information, limitation of scope, inadequacy or lack of proper records.

[Summary of Audit Opinions]

The following audit opinions were expressed for the year ended 30 June, 2024.

[Performance Audits]

A Performance Audit is an independent examination of a programme, function, operation, or management systems and procedures of a public entity to assess the Efficiency, Economy and Effectiveness and make recommendations for improvement.

Our performance audits for the year covered various Sectors, including Health, Education, Environment Protection, Energy, Agriculture, Water and Natural Resources, General Economic and Commercial Affairs, and Public Administration and Internal Affairs.

Additionally, we undertook annual assessments for the Financing Locally Led Climate Action Programme (FLLoCA) in 45 counties and also 2 consolidated reports were finalised. This programme is aimed at strengthening the capacity of County Governments to deliver community driven climate resilience actions.

[Citizen Accountability Audit]

conducting participatory audits where citizens, through Civil Society Organisations (CSOs), are involved in the audit process to enhance service delivery and good governance principles.

We engaged citizens through Focused Group Discussions to obtain feedback for consideration in our audits.

In addition, we worked together with various stakeholders to review the CAA Engagement Framework to make it more relevant to the issues affecting Citizens. The Framework enhances citizen participation in governance and public audit.

[Forensic Audit]

Forensic audits seek to establish fraud, corruption or other financial improprieties and ensure those found culpable are held to account. The audits are performed on request from stakeholders or through own initiative. During the year, we completed five (5) forensic audits

[Public Debt Audit]

The audit focuses on confirming whether the Government is managing public debt in a sustainable manner. It involves carrying out financial, compliance or performance audits on public debt management.

During the year, we conducted a Public Debt audit on the Management of Cash and Domestic Debt to assess measures put in place by The National Treasury in ensuring effective cash and domestic debt management.

[Systems Assurance and Data Science]

A systems assurance audit is an independent check of an entity's IT systems to verify its efficiency, effectiveness and reliability and ensure proper controls are in place to protect its assets and data. This process builds trust and supports risk management.

We audited major government IT systems including the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS), payroll systems, the Public Debt Management System, and the eCitizen digital service platform. These audits assessed the reliability, accuracy, and security of financial transactions, and the findings directly influenced ongoing financial audits.

Additionally, we audited the Financial Inclusion Fund (Hustler Fund) and Social Protection Programmes to review disbursements of funds to beneficiaries. The reports generated actionable recommendations that reinforced ICT governance in public institutions.

[Our Contribution to Climate Action]

Climate change is a major threat to Kenya's socio-economic development. It manifests itself in the form of severe droughts and floods, which has the potential to erode the development gains achieved over the years, and threatens the attainment of national development plans.

We contributed to a multi-stakeholder programme aimed at strengthening the capacity of county governments to deliver locally-led climate resilience through the Financing Locally Led Climate Action (FLLoCA) Programmme. FLLoCA is a Government programme co-funded by the World Bank and other development partners, including the governments of Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Germany.

Our Annual Performance Assessment of the Programme in forty-five (45) counties entailed assessing whether the counties qualified for the FLLoCA Grant.  The assessment also established performance scores for the Counties to determine the amount of Grant to be disbursed.

Some of the key areas identified as having hindered some counties from fully meeting the set conditions included:

~ Failure to allocate at least 1.5% of their Net Development Budgets to the County Climate Change Fund and at least 95% of the County Climate Resilience Investment budget to resilience investment projects.

~ Failure to absorb the County Climate Change Fund as planned and budgeted for.

~ Delays in providing feedback to the Programme Implementing Unit.

~ Failure to obtain the requisite licenses prior to commencing projects.

The recommendations provided based on the results of the Annual Performance Assessment included:

[County governments should:]

~ Allocate to the County Climate Change Fund a minimum of 1.5% of their Annual Development Budget, exclusive of the County Climate Resilience Investment (CCRI) Grant and other conditional grants.

~ Allocate at least 95% of the CCRI budget to resilience investment projects.

~ Streamline the planning and procurement processes in order to improve the absorption rate of the County Climate Change Funds.

~ Ensure timely preparation and submission of the requisite reports to the Programme Implementing Unit. The reports include Financial, Grievance Redress, Monitoring and Evaluation and Environmental and Social Safeguards Progress Reports on the utilisation of the County Climate Resilience Investment Grant.

~ Undertake Environmental and Social Impact Assessments and obtain all applicable licenses prior to the commencement of the projects funded under the County Climate Change Fund (including CCRI).

Through FLLoCA Programme, counties have received approximately Kshs.21.7B for climate action as additional allocations since its inception in 2023. It is our belief that without proper guidance and accountability frameworks, funds allocated to FLLoCA Programme risk being ineffectively deployed or diverted from their intended purpose.

To strengthen oversight, we sensitised Members of Parliament on the role the Legislature should play in advocating for climate change related actions and prudent use of climate funds at the county level.

The Office continues to receive increased recognition from various stakeholders for its work on environment and climate change. During the Year, the Office participated in various forums, serving both as participants and resource persons.

[Risk Management and Legal Compliance]

We provided independent assurance on the effectiveness of governance, risk management, and internal controls. Identified gaps were addressed in line with our internal audit recommendations, supported by a robust tracking system that has strengthened process improvements.

On the legal front, we strengthened governance by developing and aligning internal policies, while providing legal expertise to support audits. Staff were sensitised on the Public Audit Act, 2015 and other legal matters to promote awareness and compliance.

Additionally, numerous information requests from government and private entities were addressed in accordance with the Access to Information Act, 2016, reinforcing transparency and accountability.

[Budgetary Allocation]

The Office was allocated Kshs.8.2B during the financial year 2024/2025, to undertake our activities as per the constitutional requirements and our Strategic Plan. This amount was, however, lower than our requirements of Kshs.10.0B leading to a shortfall of Kshs.1.8B

Over time, an increase in requests for special audits from various stakeholders, combined with an expanded audit scope, has put a strain on our limited resources, calling for urgent enhanced funding.

Parliament, aware of our need for additional resources, recommended that the funding for the Office be based on a formula of onehalf percent (0.5%) of the latest audited and approved revenue figures of the National Government. This would enhance our resourcing and lead to improved results.

We continue to engage with Parliament and The National Treasury for adequate funding to enable us effectively execute our constitutional mandate

[Goods and Services]

strategies in both in-house and outsourced

We procured goods and services worth Kshs.902M , in line with our Procurement Plan and the Public Procurement and Assets Disposal Act, 2015.

A total of KShs.101M worth of contracts were awarded to the disadvantaged groups (Youth, Women and Persons Living with Disabilities) against the target of KShs.104M . The success was attributed to deliberate efforts in allocating additional opportunities and sensitizing firms owned by the disadvantaged groups.

[Observing quality and embracing innovation]

Quality of our audit work is central to our credibility. The Office has adopted strategies aligned with  the revised Quality Monitoring Handbook and its associated policies in compliance with the updated International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI-140). The standard governs Quality Management for Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs). We apply these audits to ensure highquality.

The Office has customised working papers and adopted sector-based programmatic audit approach to ensure wholistic audit coverage.

Additionally, we have adopted a buddy system as a mentorship and coaching strategy to strengthen peer- to-peer learning and build confidence among and across audit team members.

This approach, integrated with frequent meetings to review work, providing feedback and exchange of ideas, ensures continuous development and knowledge sharing.

Alongside this, audit teams continue to embrace existing AI tools as part of the Office's commitment to innovation and the improvement of quality, accuracy and efficiency in delivery of reports.

[County Assemblies' Perception of our Work]

We conducted a survey to get feedback on our audit services from 60 Members of County Assemblies drawn from various counties.

In promoting accountability in the use and management of public funds, 88.5% of the MCAs interviewed agreed that we are a credible voice in public sector accountability, while 75.8% agreed that our reports are easily accessible, a boost to their oversight role in ensuring public funds are prudently managed.

We continue to provide support to Audit Committees at the County level and 61.3% of the respondents agreed that we are doing so, effectively.

As we strive to make a difference in the lives and livelihoods of Kenyans, 58.1% of the MCAs agreed that our reports are influencing beneficial change in the society.

In addition, 77.4% of the MCAs agreed that our reports are easy to understand.

We shall endeavour to improve our audit services and enhance communication to improve awareness and further improve on our stakeholder engagement at the Counties.

[Timely submission of audit reports]

This milestone  enables Parliament and County Assemblies to exercise effective oversight and conduct timely deliberations of the reports.

Timely submission of our audit reports is dependent on early submission of  auditees' financial statements. On this score, special mention goes to Tharaka Nithi County Executive for submitting the financial statements to the Office for audit on 29 July, 2024, ahead of the statutory deadline of 30 September, making it the first County to do so.

'This good gesture sits well with us. It means the Office of the AuditorGeneral (OAG) prepares audit reports in time, as a result of early submission of financial statements, and the Assembly gets adequate time to interrogate the reports and take appropriate action,'

The Clerk of Tharaka Nithi County Assembly Mr Paul Thirika

'Early submission of financial statements plays a crucial role in the audit process, allowing for better planning and ensuring timely submission of audit reports by the Office of the Auditor-General (OAG). Tharaka Nithi County Executive has a commendable history of prompt submissions of financial statements, consistently meeting deadlines over the past two years,'

Jane Kariuki, Director of Audit, Embu OAG Regional Office

Early submission of audit reports gives legislators adequate time to examine the reports and take appropriate action within the constitutionally prescribed timeline.  As a result, the most updated information is used for division of revenue for National and County Governments,  ensuring the allocation of resources reflects the current needs of the citizens.

[Audit Management System Upgrade]

The Office successfully upgraded and customised the Audit Management System (AMS) to align with the revised Audit Methodology and International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAIs). Key achievements included integration with data analytics tools for real-time insights and establishment of a central repository for reference materials. The Audit monitoring was enhanced by AMS through automated dashboards and enhanced workflows for improved monitoring of audit milestones.

[Transition to IPSAS Accrual]

The Office prepared its first  financial statements using the International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) Accrual reporting framework.

By embracing this shift the Office demonstrates its commitment to setting the tone in strengthening accountability and driving excellence in financial reporting in the public sector.

[Information Security: Achieving ISO 27001 and Raising the Bar]

A defining milestone for the year was the achievement of ISO/IEC 27001 certification -a globally recognised benchmark for information security management. This accomplishment followed an intensive, organisation-wide evaluation of our policies, processes, and controls, validating our commitment to safeguarding sensitive information.
heading_path: Information Security: Achieving ISO 27001 and Raising the Bar

text:
[Advisory to Parliament]

Our Auditor-General gave an advisory to National Assembly's Committee on Cohesion and Equal Opportunities, proposing amendments to the National Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008, to strengthen efforts towards promoting nationalism.

In her submission, she added that the Act hinders public institutions from effectively adhering to regulations that promote national cohesion and integration.

The Office suggested that the law should align with constitutional principles on inclusion and equal opportunities, by prioritising the inclusion of lower cadre staff and Persons Living With Disabilities (PLWDs), in government opportunities.

The Office advised that the ammendment should introduce a reservation threshold for lower job grades, similar to provisions in public procurement law.

'These changes aim to address situations where marginalised groups, minorities, women and PLWDs are underrepresented in senior roles but overrepresented in lower cadres,' Auditor-General, FCPA Nancy Gathungu, CBS

The Office was also called upon by key stakeholders, the National Assembly, the Senate, and Civil Society Organisations (CSOs), to provide expert insights into public debt management. The areas covered included the current state of public debt in the country, present and projected debt servicing expenditure, as well as their impact on government spending.

[CHALLENGES]

In executing our mandate, we experienced the following challenges:

[1. Funding shortfalls and late exchequer release]

The Office was allocated Kshs. 8.2 Billion against our requirement of Kshs.10 Billion, translating to a funding gap of Ksh.1.8 Billion. This, together with delays in exchequer release affected the implementation of planned activities. We, however, continue to seek support from The National Treasury and Parliament for enhanced budgetary allocation.
heading_path: 1. Funding shortfalls and late exchequer release

text:
[2. Expanded audit scope]

Our audit universe has been growing over the years due to increase of self-reporting entities. Additionally, growing interest of citizens in public sector accountability resulted to numerous requests for special audits by our stakeholders, on topical areas, thereby increasing our scope of work.

[3. Delay by Parliament to discuss Performance Audit reports]

Despite submitting 63 Performance Audit Reports to Parliament since 2012, only two reports have been discussed by Parliament. Performance Audit Reports give recommendations that, if implemented, would address some of the challenges the country experiences. We acknowledge that the Speaker of the National Assembly, aware of the importance of these reports in transforming the lives of Kenyans, communicated to Parliamentary Committees on 13 May 2024 to

56

prioritise discussion and adoption of performance audit reports for action.

Low Implementation of Audit Recommendations

The Office and Parliament make recommendations to enhance good governance, accountability and effective utilisation of public resources. Unfortunately, these recommendations in  some cases, are not implemented by the concerned parties. Follow-up of the FY2020/2021 Public Accounts Committee Report and 24th Public Investments Committee Report reflected that only 21% and 25% respectively, of the recommendations made by Parliament were implemented. This significantly hampered our resolve to provide audit services that impact on lives and livelihoods of the citizenry. In light of this, we have submitted recommendations to Parliament for  review of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012, to make implementation of audit recommendations mandatory for all public entities.
heading_path: 3. Delay by Parliament to discuss Performance Audit reports

text:
[5. Tight audit timelines]

Our timelines for submission of audit reports to Parliament and County Assemblies are very tight owing to a provision of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012, which gives public entities three (3) months after the end of the financial year to present their financial statements for auditing. This reduces the duration to 3 months from the 6 months constitutional timelines given to the AuditorGeneral to audit and report.

ASSESSMENT OF OUR OPERATIONS - ICBF

ANNUAL CORPORATE REPORT | 2024 - 2025

T he The African Organisation of Englishspeaking Supreme Audit Institutions (AFROSAI-E) conduct annual assessment on the performance of audit institutions, to assess their training needs. The Assessment  is based on the Institutional Capacity Building Framework (ICBF), a tool that enables SAIs to consider and prioritise their capacity building needs, gaps and challenges.

The ICBF assesses the level of development of SAIs on five domain areas:

[Â Independence and Legal Framework]

This assesses the operational, financial and administrative independence of the Auditor-General and the staff.

[Â Organisation and Management]

This focuses on the governance and leadership matters as well as operational and strategic planning.

[Â Human Resources]

This domain assesses the management and development of staff. It covers recruitment, induction, retention, recognition, performance management, training, career development and staff wellness.

[Â Audit Standards and Methodology]

This focuses on development, implementation and maintenance of appropriate up-to-date ISSAI compliant audit tools like manuals, guidelines, and templates, in accordance with the SAI's mandate and national legislative requirements.

[Â Communication and Stakeholder Management]

This domain focuses on engagement with stakeholders guided by strategies and plans that are aligned with, and in support of the strategic goals and mandate of the SAI.

The assessment sought to establish the levels of development in the five domains. The development levels were graded from Level 1 to 5, with the following explanations:

[Level 1]

This is the Foundation Level. When a SAI scores Level 1, it means the SAI exists but operations are  at rudimentary Level. The SAI is part of the executive government structure and not independent in any area. The audit work is not organised according to a strategic, annual operational or audit work plan and the work is not carried out according to the INTOSAI Code of Ethics.

[Level 2]

This is the Development Level. The SAI exists and has some legal provisions for its independence, but this provision is not adequate and the SAI is dependent on the executive for its human and financial resources. The Head of the SAI is appointed by the Executive. Access to information, discretion to select audit topics, freedom to decide on content, timing and publishing of reports can be provided by the legislation, but is not carried out without obstacles. The SAI has no direct access to Parliament to submit audit reports. Strategic, annual operational, audit, development and communication plans and the status behind these can be under planning or development but are not implemented.

[Level 3]

This is the Established Level. At this Level plans prepared or under development at Level 2 are implemented at Level 3, however improvement in some areas or in the implementation is needed. The SAI has a legislative, administrative/managerial and financial independence. The SAI reports directly to Parliament. The Head of SAI is appointed by and can only be removed by Parliament. Functional strategic and operational plans are implemented as well as important quality control requirements for the SAI as set by the SAI leadership.

[Level 4]

This is the Managed Level. At this Level full compliance with all requirements on Level 3 is achieved by the SAI. The SAI and the key stakeholders are fully satisfied at Level 4 with the implementation of plans and procedures. In addition to the conditions at level 3, the SAI is capable of managing its core business in the most cost efficient and cost-effective way.

[Level 5]

This is the Optimised Level.  The SAI complies fully with all requirements on Level 4. At this Level, the SAI is able to scan the environment and position itself and use the resources in the most proactive and value adding way. To optimise its use of resources the SAI must constantly evaluate, analyse and assess its policies, objectives, strategies, systems, procedures, capacity, the skill of its staff and the impact of its decisions.

[Artificial Intelligence (AI)]

F or effective and efficient service delivery and in line with emerging global trends, the Office will adopt the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). At the National level, the Kenya National AI Strategy (2025) sets out a vision for Kenya as a continental leader in AI, with emphasis on ethical adoption, inclusive innovation, and strong governance.

In alignment, the Office is at an advanced level in developing an AI Strategy to establish a framework to responsibly integrate AI into audit and administrative processes, build institutional capacity to harness and regulate AI, ensure compliance with global and National standards, and contribute to Kenya's digital transformation agenda while safeguarding audit independence and public trust.

[Electronic Submission of Financial Statements]

In pursuit of the Office's commitment to innovation and digitisation for enhanced efficiency, we envision the adoption of electronic submission of financial statements by auditees. This shall streamline the audit process by enhancing timely access to standardised financial data, enable its realtime validation and reduce delays associated with physical submissions.

Additionally, this shall boost data security in line with ISO 27001 in the receipt and storage of sensitive data. This initiative shall align with global good practices in public sector auditing while improving efficiency and reinforcing transparency and accountability.

[Citizen Accountability Audit Mobile App]

The App is meant to compliment other avenues of engaging with citizens for robust and targeted dissemination of results of Citizen Accountability Audits (CAA) operations and policies. The portal and the mobile application will improve OAG's visibility and support the institution's outreach to stakeholders and citizens at large. It will also be used as a knowledge and resource sharing platform,

cataloguing and disseminating information for the benefit of citizens. In addition, the Office of the Auditor-General of the Republic of Kenya has been selected by AFROSAI as one the countries in Africa to implement technologybased solutions to engage citizens and obtain feedback.  This programme is being supported by GIZ South Africa.

[Development and rollout of the Knowledge Management System (KMS):]

The Office plans to deploy Knowledge Management Systems, a structured and accessible repository to facilitate capture, storage and retrieval of verifiable institutional information to enhance continuity and efficiency.

Additionally, the Office is in the process of digitising the library to expand digital access to learning and research materials to support staff development.

Our one-stop-shop central hub for resources, collaboration, and internal communication platform is in the pipeline to foster a more connected, faster and digitally oriented and informed staff. The platform will eliminate manual processes in our operations, giving our staff an opportunity to access Office services at the click of a button.
